items.text: I consider myself as a intraday swing trader … a mix of Minervini style swing trading in intraday
I only do long side trading, I don't short.
I'm a 100% technical trader … I don't look at the news much … I just trade the price and volume action.
I developed five to six go-to chart setups.

the watch list scanner that I developed … the price of the stock anything from 50 cents to $100 … volume should be minimum 1 million volume and then percentage change from the previous day at least minimum 25% change … then it comes to my small caps watch list.
the minimum is 1 million volume in my scanner … the more the better.
I created my own scanner, small cap volatility scanner … any stock which is above 50 cents and max $100 and the volume should be 1 million and at least up by 25%, show me all these stocks.
I prefer more liquid stocks … volume is a must … I don't take the trades which have less volume even though the price move is big.

ThinkorSwim has this pre-market movers scanner … I sort by volume … and also I look at the percentage gainers [ToS built-in] … as soon as the market opens this gets filled … I sort by the percentage change, see which are the biggest movers.

the bigger the volume the better … 1 million volume and the price is only $2 and it's just one bar in five minutes and after that it was fading out — I'm not interested at all. Now the volume is picking up, 2.6 million, 3 million … the volume is sustaining and it's increasing … this gradual increase in volume catches my attention.
when the float is low when there is volume there can be halt-up kind of magnitude move.
the reversal squeeze happens only in the low float stocks, the lower the float the better.
He reads the float off the ThinkorSwim "shares" column. This tab uses the yfinance float, else shares outstanding — the chip says which.
I tried 1 minute 3 minute 5 minute 15 minutes … I concluded on the five minute … 5 minute is my favorite.
I usually switch between five and 15 minutes.
this is the 9 EMA, this is the 21 EMA.
I'll have a 9 EMA and 21 EMA, I have this price and then this volume, that's all. My chart has nothing else, I don't have VWAP or ADRs. I'm strictly price and volume based.
even though this is a 5 minute chart I always go and look at the daily … draw the support and resistance … I zoom out.
I align my intraday thesis with the daily … continuation run … more confidence.
it has a history of prior runs, history of squeezes
When the daily and the intraday have the congruence, the move is going to be exponential

in the pre-market I'll see what's moving, I'll open my scanner … ToS pre-market mover scanner and the Zendoo online scanner … if it's making some noise in pre-market I put them in my watch list and also there will be some stocks which make after hours moves from the past day, I'll keep them as well
I don't take trades for the first 15 minutes after the market opens … I want to see the direction … whenever I tried trading right at the open most of the times I ended up in losses.
at a time I'll be watching closely four or five stocks
towards the market close sometimes this will squeeze up … and squeeze up after hours too, that's why I'll actively watch it towards the close.
most of the stocks make a big move after hours
in the post market the run will be much smoother, the volume will be low, but the magnitude of the squeezes will be huge
limit orders only … slippage … I trade with less size after and pre-market.
if most stocks are in downtrend, the volume is low like in summers, I don't look at the screens, I take the day off.
in a good day there will be a couple of 100%+ runners
On a very bad day the maximum runners would be 30%–40% and two, three, four of them, and then others 10%, 20% — that tells me the market is not strong for my strategy, it's quiet.
He honours that read: in quiet weeks he trades very little.
if the market is good on average two, three, four trades per day

all these setups have the same criteria: good demand, very shallow pullback with low volume, very constructive action, and if it takes the previous highs — enter; stop loss would be the low of the base.
strong demand, goes sideways at the top of the bars, volume subsides in those bars, and if it reclaims the highs — this is the concept of all the moves.
gradual increase in price along with gradual increase in volume [2–3 green bars], then almost sideways or very shallow pullback with less volume compared to the left side.
the pullback is one bar, usually two to three bars … it happens within 10 minutes and takes off, this is the fastest.

at least two big green bars (three is good) with a good price increase; the next few bars consolidate around the top with low-volume bars; entry at the top of the pullback bar, exit [stop] at the bottom of it
Entry: the break of the pullback bar's high. Stop: that bar's low.

extension of bull flag where the left side won't be that strong, only two green bars or one green bar … it waits more and honors the 9 EMA whenever it pulls back … within the pullback the volume will be considerably low compared to the green bars
it will honor the EMAs — the 9 EMA touch and go, touch and go, ride it higher
Entry: the high of the bar that kissed the 9 EMA. Stop: below the low of the previous bar.

left side strong, gradually goes sideways with low volume pullback towards the high of the price action, shallow very clean pullback, and when the 9 EMA and 21 EMA merge around that area then slowly the momentum starts … risk very tiny below the previous bar.
If I flip to 15 minutes it looks even better.
not something that happens very often.
this is like a bull flag in the 15 minute chart … goes sideways at the very high of the price, volume subsiding, then if it picks up I take the call.

left side good demand, then it honors the 21 EMA when it pulls back with less volume … in each cycle it honors the 21 EMA and the volatility contracts in each cycle … the entry would be the top of this [last] cycle and the stop loss the low of this cycle … it should have this uptrend look.

happens only mostly in low float stocks, the lower the float the better … tennis ball action: whenever there is a drop it tries to squeeze up, whenever it hits the ground it [reverses] back hard … when the volume picks up it squeezes, explosive moves
the pullback is very gradual, all at the top of this bar with gradual decrease in volume … as soon as the selling pressure is reduced and the demand kicks in, explosive.
the lower the float the better; good volume; already strong demand, especially when the price goes down it almost immediately comes up like a ball under the water
this time the sell-off was big and the [reversal] back was quick.
it has that look of a ball [reversing] back.
a halt is nothing but too much demand in a very short time
if it moves sideways with less volume and forms another base, high chance it has an even bigger move
Entry: when it takes the highs after the quiet base. Stop: the base low.

when it's breaking out I anticipate the volume is going to follow … I just look at the price … I'll enter right at the break [of the previous bar's high]; sometimes I wait for the bar to close and enter in the next bar.
most of my exits [stops] are below the low of the previous bar, always; tight risk-reward entries always.
if it stops me out I won't re-enter right then … I need at least a couple of bars to see whether the action is good.
I don't want to be the first one in; I want the price and volume to prove it.
I want to be more careful and have this [higher] high as my buy point.
Progressive exposure: winning → bigger size, drawdown → smaller; an A+ setup → double size.
if $2,000 is the loss in one trade, next trade I cut to $1,000 … then $500
if I'm in a −10% or −15% drawdown: next five trades should be only −5% together

track_record.rule_text: GG's trade math (your answer, 2026-10-16). Entry = the trigger the alert gave: the first 1-minute bar from 09:45 ET to 16:00 ET (your answer: from 09:45 ET only) that starts 30 s or more after the alert and trades at or above the trigger fills — at the trigger, or at that bar's open when it opened above it (a gap fills at the open). WIN = a later 1-minute high reaches the fill +1R (R = trigger − stop, as the alert gave them) before any low touches the stop. LOSS = the stop is touched first; a bar that touches both counts as a loss, and so does a stop touched in the fill minute. Same session = through 16:00 ET on the alert's day (an alert at or after 16:00 ET: through 16:00 ET of the next market day, its first regular session); through next session = the same walk to 16:00 ET of the market day after that, after-hours and pre-market prints included. The % is the best high after the fill against the fill; the small % is the column's last close against the fill. No entry and no plan are listed, never counted; a thin R (under 0.5% of the trigger) is graded and kept out of the %.

items.text: I consider myself as a intraday swing trader … a mix of Minervini style swing trading in intraday
I only do long side trading, I don't short.
I'm a 100% technical trader … I don't look at the news much … I just trade the price and volume action.
I developed five to six go-to chart setups.

the watch list scanner that I developed … the price of the stock anything from 50 cents to $100 … volume should be minimum 1 million volume and then percentage change from the previous day at least minimum 25% change … then it comes to my small caps watch list.
the minimum is 1 million volume in my scanner … the more the better.
I created my own scanner, small cap volatility scanner … any stock which is above 50 cents and max $100 and the volume should be 1 million and at least up by 25%, show me all these stocks.
I prefer more liquid stocks … volume is a must … I don't take the trades which have less volume even though the price move is big.

ThinkorSwim has this pre-market movers scanner … I sort by volume … and also I look at the percentage gainers [ToS built-in] … as soon as the market opens this gets filled … I sort by the percentage change, see which are the biggest movers.

the bigger the volume the better … 1 million volume and the price is only $2 and it's just one bar in five minutes and after that it was fading out — I'm not interested at all. Now the volume is picking up, 2.6 million, 3 million … the volume is sustaining and it's increasing … this gradual increase in volume catches my attention.
when the float is low when there is volume there can be halt-up kind of magnitude move.
the reversal squeeze happens only in the low float stocks, the lower the float the better.
He reads the float off the ThinkorSwim "shares" column. This tab uses the yfinance float, else shares outstanding — the chip says which.
I tried 1 minute 3 minute 5 minute 15 minutes … I concluded on the five minute … 5 minute is my favorite.
I usually switch between five and 15 minutes.
this is the 9 EMA, this is the 21 EMA.
I'll have a 9 EMA and 21 EMA, I have this price and then this volume, that's all. My chart has nothing else, I don't have VWAP or ADRs. I'm strictly price and volume based.
even though this is a 5 minute chart I always go and look at the daily … draw the support and resistance … I zoom out.
I align my intraday thesis with the daily … continuation run … more confidence.
it has a history of prior runs, history of squeezes
When the daily and the intraday have the congruence, the move is going to be exponential

in the pre-market I'll see what's moving, I'll open my scanner … ToS pre-market mover scanner and the Zendoo online scanner … if it's making some noise in pre-market I put them in my watch list and also there will be some stocks which make after hours moves from the past day, I'll keep them as well
I don't take trades for the first 15 minutes after the market opens … I want to see the direction … whenever I tried trading right at the open most of the times I ended up in losses.
at a time I'll be watching closely four or five stocks
towards the market close sometimes this will squeeze up … and squeeze up after hours too, that's why I'll actively watch it towards the close.
most of the stocks make a big move after hours
in the post market the run will be much smoother, the volume will be low, but the magnitude of the squeezes will be huge
limit orders only … slippage … I trade with less size after and pre-market.
if most stocks are in downtrend, the volume is low like in summers, I don't look at the screens, I take the day off.
in a good day there will be a couple of 100%+ runners

happens only mostly in low float stocks, the lower the float the better … tennis ball action: whenever there is a drop it tries to squeeze up, whenever it hits the ground it [reverses] back hard … when the volume picks up it squeezes, explosive moves
the pullback is very gradual, all at the top of this bar with gradual decrease in volume … as soon as the selling pressure is reduced and the demand kicks in, explosive.
the lower the float the better; good volume; already strong demand, especially when the price goes down it almost immediately comes up like a ball under the water
this time the sell-off was big and the [reversal] back was quick.
it has that look of a ball [reversing] back.
a halt is nothing but too much demand in a very short time
if it moves sideways with less volume and forms another base, high chance it has an even bigger move
Entry: when it takes the highs after the quiet base. Stop: the base low.

when it's breaking out I anticipate the volume is going to follow … I just look at the price … I'll enter right at the break [of the previous bar's high]; sometimes I wait for the bar to close and enter in the next bar.
most of my exits [stops] are below the low of the previous bar, always; tight risk-reward entries always.
if it stops me out I won't re-enter right then … I need at least a couple of bars to see whether the action is good.
I don't want to be the first one in; I want the price and volume to prove it.
I want to be more careful and have this [higher] high as my buy point.
Progressive exposure: winning → bigger size, drawdown → smaller; an A+ setup → double size.
if $2,000 is the loss in one trade, next trade I cut to $1,000 … then $500
if I'm in a −10% or −15% drawdown: next five trades should be only −5% together

track_record.rule_text: GG's trade math (your answer, 2026-10-16). Entry = the trigger the alert gave: the first 1-minute bar from 09:45 ET to 16:00 ET (your answer: from 09:45 ET only) that starts 30 s or more after the alert and trades at or above the trigger fills — at the trigger, or at that bar's open when it opened above it (a gap fills at the open). WIN = a later 1-minute high reaches the fill +1R (R = trigger − stop, as the alert gave them) before any low touches the stop. LOSS = the stop is touched first; a bar that touches both counts as a loss, and so does a stop touched in the fill minute. Same session = through 16:00 ET on the alert's day (an alert at or after 16:00 ET: through 16:00 ET of the next market day, its first regular session); through next session = the same walk to 16:00 ET of the market day after that, after-hours and pre-market prints included. The % is the best high after the fill against the fill; the small % is the column's last close against the fill. No entry and no plan are listed, never counted; a thin R (under 0.5% of the trigger) is graded and kept out of the %.
